title: Love that stays in the road
hookLine: Krishna's chariot leaves for Mathura, and the gopis stand in the road until the dust is gone
carry: viraha: longing is a way of loving
tomorrow: what did Akrura see when he went under the river?

cards: The news gets around the village overnight. By morning everyone knows: Akrura has come from Mathura, and he's taking Krishna and Balarama with him.

The cowherd men load carts with pots of milk and butter as gifts for the king. And the gopis, who ran into the forest at the sound of a flute, stand in the road beside the chariot. This time there's nothing to run toward.

teach.h: THEY BLAME THE CREATOR, AND AKRURA.
teach.b: The Bhagavata gives the gopis a long, raw lament, and doesn't tidy it up. They blame the creator, who brings people together and pulls them apart for no reason, like a child playing and spoiling the game.
They turn on Akrura too. His name means not cruel, they say, and it doesn't fit: he's come to carry off the one thing they have.

They imagine the women of Mathura, who will see Krishna every day now, and wonder whether a city boy will remember village girls. Then they stop caring what anyone thinks, and cry out his names in the road.
Krishna sees them and sends back word through a messenger, as the text puts it: I will come back.

And the gopis stand watching until the flag on the chariot and the dust behind it are gone. Look at the shape of this week: hearing him, emptying out for him, running to him as they were, finding him beside every one.
Now the same love has nowhere to go, and it doesn't stop.
Hindu devotion has a name for this: viraha, love in separation.
Many teachers, especially in the Krishna traditions of Braj and Bengal, hold that longing for God while apart isn't a failure of love but one of its deepest forms, because the mind never leaves him.
Poets like Surdas filled songbooks with the gopis' longing. The story will come back to these women.

how: The gopis' longing after Krishna leaves, viraha, is a great theme of devotional poetry and song, sung in bhajans and kirtan and at the close of many kathas.

o: the morning Krishna's chariot leaves the village for Mathura
the day Krishna's family moves to a new pasture
the day the cowherds flee a flood toward Mathura

games.q: this week in Vraja — tap the pairs.
p: empty of ego, for his breath

s: the gopis let Krishna go quietly
they lament aloud, blaming the creator and Akrura, and call out his names in the road.
Krishna sends word that he will come back
as the chariot leaves, he sends a messenger with that promise.
in bhakti, missing God means the love has failed
many teachers call viraha, love in separation, one of devotion's deepest forms.

games.q: you're a gopi in the road. the chariot is about to leave for Mathura, with Krishna in it. what do you do?
o: say a polite goodbye and go home.
cry out his names and stand watching until the dust is gone.
games.why: the gopis lament and call his names, then stand in the road until the flag and the dust disappear. that longing, viraha, is love that doesn't stop.

practice: Songs of viraha are sung wherever Krishna is loved. Bring to mind someone who is far from you, on a trip, in a new city, or further, and let yourself be one of the ones standing in the road; if there's an ache, don't push it away.
If you pray, let the ache become a call, and say Krishna's name, or God's, softly, the way the gopis called his names. If you don't, hold that person in mind with thanks, without asking for anything.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Vrindavan. The morning Krishna's chariot leaves for Mathura, and the gopis watch until the flag and the dust are gone.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Akrura, 'not cruel.' In the story the gopis say the name doesn't fit him.

carryVoice: Your line: viraha, longing is a way of loving. Tomorrow: what did Akrura see under the river? See you then.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.39, the gopis' lament at Krishna's departure and his message that he will return
